front: List the pipeline stages from data collection to evaluation.
back: Data collection, data preparation, exploratory data analysis, feature engineering, training, tuning and evaluation. The problem definition comes first, deployment and monitoring come after.

front: Which stage turns raw data into useful inputs such as 'days since last order'?
back: Feature engineering. Good features often improve a model more than a fancier algorithm does.

front: What are hyperparameters, and which stage adjusts them?
back: Settings you choose before training, such as how long to train. The tuning stage adjusts them to improve results.

front: What are the three data splits and what is each for?
back: Training data to learn from, validation data to tune, and test data for a final honest check on unseen examples.

front: Why must evaluation use data the model has never seen?
back: To show whether it will work in the real world and to guard against overfitting. A high training score alone proves little.

front: What are the three main sources of a model for a project?
back: A proprietary model used through a managed service, an open-source pre-trained model, or a custom model you train yourself on your own data.

front: Why is training your own foundation model rarely the right choice?
back: It is very costly. Adapting a pre-trained model gives a head start. Training your own suits narrow tasks with unique data, like a fraud model.

front: What advantage do open-source pre-trained models offer over a proprietary managed API?
back: More control over hosting and customization, at the price of more work. The weights are published, so you can run and, where allowed, fine-tune them.

front: Why does Cairnway train its own fraud model but use a Bedrock model for Trailmate?
back: Fraud data is unique to Cairnway and the task is narrow. Trailmate needs general language ability, which an existing foundation model already provides.

front: What is the main difference between a managed API and a self-hosted API for a model?
back: With a managed API the provider hosts and runs the model, so you do little operational work. Self-hosting means you deploy, size, secure and update it yourself.

front: Which clue words point to a managed API such as Amazon Bedrock?
back: 'Without managing infrastructure', 'fastest to market' and 'least effort'.

front: Which clue words point to self-hosting a model?
back: 'Specific open-source model', 'full control' and 'custom hardware'. Self-hosting runs on a SageMaker AI endpoint or EC2.

front: How do cost patterns differ between managed and self-hosted models?
back: Managed APIs are typically pay per use, such as per token. Self-hosted models cost server time while they run, even when idle, unless scaled down.

front: Which feature builds labeled training data with a human workforce, and what is its status?
back: SageMaker Ground Truth. AWS says it is closed to new customers, so the exam tests what it is for.

front: Which service stores features with an online store for fast reads and an offline store for training?
back: SageMaker Feature Store. Using one store keeps training and live scoring on the same feature definitions.

front: How do SageMaker Pipelines and SageMaker Model Registry differ?
back: Pipelines automates the workflow steps from processing to deployment. Model Registry catalogs model versions and tracks approval status.

front: Which tool prepares data with little to no code, and where is it integrated now?
back: SageMaker Data Wrangler, which AWS says is now integrated into SageMaker Canvas.

front: Which tool checks bias and explains predictions, and which watches a model in production?
back: SageMaker Clarify checks bias and explains predictions. SageMaker Model Monitor watches production models for drift. Both are closed to new customers.

front: How do Amazon Quick and Kiro differ in purpose?
back: Quick is an AI workspace for business users to consume AI and data. Kiro is an agentic engineering system for developers to build software around models.

front: What is MLOps?
back: It applies DevOps habits to ML: automate, test and monitor the whole lifecycle so models are delivered and kept healthy reliably.

front: What is drift, and how does Cairnway's fraud model show it?
back: Drift is when the world changes so a model's inputs or right answers shift and accuracy falls. Fraudsters changed tactics and recall dropped.

front: Accuracy falls after deployment. Is this a training bug?
back: Usually not. It is typically drift. The answer is monitoring plus retraining through the automated pipeline.

front: Why do MLOps teams track experiments?
back: So results from different data sets, features and settings can be compared and reproduced later.

front: What does managing technical debt mean in ML projects?
back: Avoiding quick hacks such as hand-run steps and undocumented data that slow every later change. Pay it down with versioning, documentation and automation.

front: What does production readiness include before a model launches?
back: It is tested, secured, documented, approved and cost-checked, with a rollback plan. A registry approval step supports this.

front: What do precision and recall each measure?
back: Precision asks how often a 'positive' prediction is right (TP divided by TP plus FP). Recall asks how many real positives were found (TP divided by TP plus FN).

front: Why can high accuracy mislead for fraud detection?
back: With rare fraud, a model that always says legitimate can score 95% accuracy yet catch no fraud. Its recall is zero.

front: When should you focus on recall rather than precision?
back: When missing a real case is costly, such as fraud or disease. Focus on precision when false alarms are costly.

front: When is the F1 score the right metric?
back: When precision and recall both matter and classes are unbalanced. It is one number that balances the two.

front: A model has excellent F1 but loses money. How should you judge it?
back: On both model metrics and business metrics. Technical metrics say if it works, and business metrics say if it is worth it.

front: Name four business metrics for evaluating an ML model.
back: Cost per user or prediction, development costs, customer feedback and return on investment (ROI).
